title: Terms of Reference (ToR) for Software Development Firm
raw_text: Terms of Reference (TOR) for Software Development Firm Project Title: From one-o+ mapping to a living service ecosystem: Development of an Interactive Actor Mapping and Referral System for Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS). Contracting authority Institute for Community Based Sociotherapy (ICBS), in coordination with Rwanda Biomedical Centre – Mental Health Division (RBC-MHD) Ministry of Health (MoH) Assignment Design, development, deployment, training, handover and support of a secure national digital platform for all national and international MHPSS actors in Rwanda Primary users Government institutions, MHPSS actors, service providers and authorized referral users 1. Background Rwanda has progressively decentralized mental health care and integrated it into primary care. Rwanda Biomedical Centre - Mental Health Division (RBC-MHD) also coordinates a growing network of governmental and non-governmental actors providing community-based Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services, that intersect with other wider peacebuilding and development interventions. Current information on MHPSS actors, services and referral pathways is fragmented across separate and often static systems and mappings. As projects, focal persons and geographic coverage change, mappings quickly become outdated. This limits coordination, creates duplication and gaps, and makes referrals and follow-up di+icult to manage. RBC-MHD and its partners, in partnership with other relevant ministries and government institutions, therefore seek a secure, sustainable platform that turns one-o+ mapping into a continuously updated service ecosystem, with the potential to work inter-ministerial. 2. Objectives The assignment is to design, develop, deploy and support a user-friendly national digital platform that improves coordination among actors that o+er services related to MHPSS and other relevant sectors, and strengthens referral and counter-referral pathways. The platform will: maintain an up-to-date registry of actors, services, activities and geographic coverage; identify service, geographic and resource gaps and reduce duplication; enable secure referrals, follow-up, feedback and counter-referrals; provide aggregated dashboards, maps, data visulization and reports for planning and policy; support data quality, accountability and organizational learning; and remain scalable, interoperable and maintainable by the responsible institutions. 3. Scope of Work 3.1 Requirements and co-design The firm will conduct stakeholder consultations, document business processes and data flows, define user roles and permissions, assess existing systems and integration points, and agree the final functional and non-functional requirements with RBC-MHD, ICBS and other identified partners. The approved System Requirements Specification (SRS) will be the baseline for development and acceptance. 3.2 Core platform modules Module Minimum purpose Actor registry and service directory Validated profiles covering organizational mandates, services, target groups, activities, staffing, geographic coverage and relevant resources. Interactive map National and subnational visualization of actors, services, gaps and agreed hotspots using aggregated, non-sensitive data. Dashboards and reports Configurable indicators and comparisons for coordination, monitoring, trends and decision-making, including agreed activity and referral statistics. User and organization management Registration, validation and administration of organizations and users, with role-based permissions for public users, organizational users and administrators, validators, referral users, government administrators and technical administrators. Referral and counter-referral Secure creation, receipt, acceptance or decline, status tracking, feedback, completion or closure, and counter-referral, with an audit trail and aggregated reporting. System administration Configuration, data validation, audit logs, backups, access management and operational monitoring. 3.3 Data management and access Provide a public area with general information and aggregated dashboards, and secure areas for registered and authorized users. Allow each organization to manage its own information and view approved information from other actors according to access rules. Preserve previous records and a complete history of changes rather than overwriting data. Apply data minimization: referrals must collect only information necessary for referral and follow-up, with sensitive data restricted to authorized users. Include data-validation and quality-control workflows and require users to accept an information-access policy. 3.4 Interoperability, hosting and sustainability The platform must support secure data exchange with relevant current and future government systems, where authorized and technically feasible. The firm will propose standards, documented APIs and integration methods; document data structures and procedures; and avoid unnecessary dependence on proprietary technology. Specific integrations will be confirmed in the SRS. The firm will propose a hosting and publication approach compatible with government requirements, including access through relevant institutional websites or portals. The architecture must support nationwide use, future modules and handover to RBC and/or another designated government institution. 4. Functional and non-functional requirements The solution must: be responsive on computers, tablets and mobile devices and support commonly used browsers; provide an intuitive, accessible interface and configurable language options agreed during inception; scale to additional users, organizations, services, locations, data volumes and modules without complete redevelopment; maintain acceptable performance and availability as usage grows; • use secure authentication, role-based access, session controls and multi-factor authentication for administrators and other high-risk roles; encrypt data in transit and, where appropriate, at rest; maintain audit logs, version histories, automated backups and tested recovery procedures; support vulnerability assessment, security testing and incident-response procedures; and comply with applicable Rwandan data protection, security and accessibility requirements. A final security assessment is required before go-live. All critical and high-risk vulnerabilities must be resolved before final acceptance. 5. Deliverables and acceptance All deliverables require review and formal approval by RBC-MHD and ICBS. The firm must address comments within agreed timelines. Approval will consider completeness, technical quality, consistency with the SRS and incorporation of stakeholder feedback. Payments are made only after formal approval of the relevant milestone. # Deliverable Minimum content 1 Inception report Understanding of the assignment; methodology; work plan and milestones; stakeholder engagement; risks and mitigation. Present for validation within 30 days of contract signature. 2 SRS and system design Approved functional and technical requirements, roles, workflows, data flows, architecture, database schemas, APIs, security design, integrations and user-interface mock-ups. 3 Monthly progress reports Progress, stakeholder engagement, decisions, issues, risks, mitigation and next steps. 4 Prototype / proof of concept Demonstration of core workflows, dashboard concepts, data integration and user interaction; revised following stakeholder feedback. 5 Configured functional platform Approved modules operational and ready for UAT, meeting agreed functional, security, performance and usability requirements. 6 Security and governance framework Security controls, data governance, ownership and access rules, data-sharing arrangements, incident handling, retention, archiving and secure deletion. 7 Testing and UAT package Functional, integration, performance, security and data validation results; UAT plan, issue log, resolutions and approved final adjustments. # Deliverable Minimum content 8 Training and support materials Administrator and user manuals, technical documentation, multiple in-person trainings with users of the system and initial help-desk/troubleshooting support. 9 Final report and handover package Final report; source code; schemas; APIs; configuration and deployment files; test records; manuals; administrative access; and enhancement recommendations. 10 Support and maintenance plan Warranty and included support period; channels and hours; incident response and resolution targets; escalation; defect correction; patches; upgrades; enhancement process; and estimated annual costs thereafter. 11 Close-out and knowledge transfer Formal handover, close-out workshop and practical transfer to RBC's IT team and other designated staff. 6. Firm qualifications and proposed team The firm must demonstrate substantial experience and expertise in developing large-scale, interactive information systems with a focus on data integration, security, an interoperability. We expect the following qualifications: at least five years of relevant software development and systems-integration experience; successful delivery of comparable management information systems, preferably for government, social protection, health, mental health or NGO programmes; experience with scalable architecture, databases, APIs, data warehousing, analytics and secure interoperability; knowledge of data protection, privacy, cybersecurity and secure software-development practices; capacity to manage multi-stakeholder projects using an agile or iterative approach; and experience in consultation, change management, training and institutional knowledge transfer. The proposed team should cover project management, business and systems analysis, software architecture and development, database and integration engineering, user experience design, cybersecurity, testing and quality assurance, training and support. Familiarity with Rwanda's institutional and technical environment is strongly preferred. 7. Proposal requirements Technical and financial proposals should include: the firm's understanding of the assignment and proposed solution; methodology, development approach, stakeholder engagement and change management plan; proposed architecture, interoperability, security, hosting and sustainability approach; work plan, milestones, dependencies, risks and quality-assurance arrangements; team structure, roles, availability, CVs and relevant certifications; evidence of comparable assignments and references; itemized costs for development, testing, training, deployment and support; and warranty, maintenance, licensing, recurring fees and estimated long-term operating costs. 8. Proposed payment schedule Payment Milestone 20% Approval of the inception report and SRS. 20% Approval of the system design and prototype / proof of concept. 25% Delivery of the functional core platform and interactive dashboard, ready for testing. 20% Successful testing, UAT, quality assurance and training. 15% Project closure, knowledge transfer and final handover of all documentation and support plans. 9. Evaluation criteria Proposals will be evaluated on: Criterion What will be assessed Technical experience Comparable systems; data integration, APIs, analytics and cybersecurity; relevant sector and Rwanda experience. Understanding Clear interpretation of the objectives, users, workflows, interoperability and data-protection requirements. Methodology Feasible iterative approach, stakeholder participation, work plan, risk management, quality assurance, training and support. Team Relevant qualifications, experience, roles, availability and certifications of key personnel. Cost and sustainability Transparent and proportionate costs, value for money, licensing implications, recurring costs and long-term maintainability. 10. Data protection, ownership and licensing All data must be processed in accordance with applicable Rwandan data protection law and approved governance arrangements. Access to personal or sensitive information must be limited to authorized users and based on documented roles and purposes. Upon final payment, RBC and/or another designated government institution will have exclusive ownership of all project-specific deliverables, including source code, database structures, architecture, APIs, configuration and deployment files, interface designs, documentation, training materials, testing records, administrative accounts, and any domain or hosting accounts procured under the project. The firm must disclose all proposed third-party, open-source and proprietary components, including licence terms, restrictions, recurring fees and maintenance implications. No component that creates unnecessary vendor lock-in or prevents future operation, transfer, modification or development may be used without prior written approval. 11. Application process and submission guidelines Interested software development firms must submit their complete proposals electronically to tender@icbs.ngo, addressed to Mr. Diogene Karangwa, General Lead of the Institute for Community Based Sociotherapy, by 28th October 2026. Late submissions or proposals sent through alternative channels will not be considered for evaluation. The subject line of the email should clearly state: "Proposal: Interactive Actor Mapping – [Your Company Name]". Required Submission Package To be considered for evaluation, applicants must submit two separate files: 1. Technical Proposal Company Profile: A brief overview of the firm, legal registration documents, and evidence of financial stability. Relevant Experience: Case studies or references from at least three (3) similar projects, ideally involving secure national digital platforms, referral systems, or health-related ecosystems. Proposed Methodology: A detailed technical approach demonstrating how the firm will design, develop, deploy, and support the platform according to the objectives. Project Timeline & Work Plan: A clear roadmap including key milestones, deliverables, and quality assurance processes. Team Composition: CVs and professional certifications of the core team members (e.g., Lead Architect, Frontend/Backend Developers, UX/UI Designer, Project Manager) who will be assigned to this project. 2. Financial Proposal Itemized Budget: A detailed breakdown of costs related to development, licensing, training, handover, and ongoing technical support. Payment Schedule: Proposed payment milestones tied directly to the project deliverables outlined in the technical work plan. 3. Administrative documents Company full registration certificate Valid tax clearance certificate Valid RSSB clearance certificate

title: Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Recruitment of a Consultancy to Conduct a Digital Market and Digital Skills Gap Assessment Across the Sama Countries
raw_text: TERMS OF REFERENCE Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Recruitment of a Consultancy to Conduct a Digital Market and Digital Skills Gap Assessment across the SAMA Countries (Under the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme, Across the six SAMA countries: Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia) Client / Contracting entity Smart Africa Secretariat 10th Floor, Career Centre Building KG 541 ST, Kigali, Rwanda, P.O. Box: 4913 Tel: +250 788 300 581/+250788822155 Email: tenderenquiries@smartafrica.org | www.smartafrica.org RFP # 157/S.A/SAMA/RFP/10/2026 Programme Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Assignment title Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis and Digital Skills Gap Assessment for the Digital Market, SAMA Interventions 1 and 2 Assignment structure One consultancy awarded as a single package comprising two coordinated components. Bidders must demonstrate distinct technical expertise for each Component and may propose a consortium or specialist team arrangements to ensure adequate depth across both components. A single contract will be awarded for the full assignment. Geographic coverage Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia Languages English and French, with local-language data collection where required Release date 08/10/2026 Closing date 09/11/2026 at 17:00 Kigali time (CAT / UTC+2) Contact Enquiries: tenderenquiries@smartafrica.org |Submissions: procurement@smartafrica.org Introduction and General Background 1.1 About the Smart Africa Alliance The Smart Africa Alliance is a bold and innovative commitment from African Heads of State and Government to accelerate sustainable socio-economic development on the continent, with the vision of transforming Africa into a Single Digital Market by 2030. Established through its Manifesto, a collaborative effort among African nations, the African Union, the Economic Commission for Africa, the African Development Bank, the World Bank, the International Telecommunication Union, the private sector, and academic and research institutions, the Alliance was endorsed by African leaders in 2014 and has since garnered the support of 42 African countries representing over one billion people. The Smart Africa Secretariat, headquartered in Kigali, Rwanda, coordinates continental programmes that support digital market integration, policy harmonization, institutional strengthening, and innovation-ecosystem development across Member States, placing information and communications technologies at the core of national and continental socio-economic development. More information: https://smartafrica.org 1.2 About Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme Smart Africa Alliance curated the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA), an initiative that brings in nexus between digital innovation – entrepreneurship, digital skills and knowledge, and strengthening policy and regulatory environment for digitization of markets while impacting youth with a particular focus on young women. SAMA Programme is a four-year, multi-country initiative supported by the Mastercard Foundation, running from 2026 through 2029. The Program aims to unlock dignified and fulfilling work opportunities for 35,584 young people, with a target of 70% young women, 5% persons with disabilities, and 5% refugees/internally displaced persons, by improving access to digital markets for economically disadvantaged youth, particularly young women small traders. The Programme is implemented across six countries: Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia. The program responds to systemic challenges in Africa’s informal economy, where approximately 90% of workers are informal and youth, who make up 75% of the population, face interlinked barriers such as limited digital connectivity, financial exclusion, inadequate market access, and digital skills gaps. SAMA builds on Smart Africa’s existing digital initiatives such as SANIA, SADA, SATA, SWG etc and aligns with the organisation’s vision for Africa’s Single Digital Market by 2030 as well as the African Union’s vision, ensuring that program efforts complement broader continental strategies for inclusive digital transformation. 1.2.1 SAMA Strategic Pillars SAMA is built around three interconnected strategic pillars to drive inclusive growth: a) Entrepreneurship and digital innovation, b) Youth Digital Skills, and c) Institutional Capacity Building. In practice, this translates to: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation by supporting youth-led tech solutions that reduce market barriers for informal traders. Youth Digital Skills Development by providing digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills training to young persons, especially young women, to improve their employability and enterprise growth. Strengthening Institutions and Policy by working with governments and regional bodies to harmonize policies, improve regulatory environments, and build institutional capacity for a unified digital market. 1.2.2 SAMA Target Personas The Programme’s human-centred design is built around and targets three distinct groups of young persons in Africa: Small market trader or “Aisha”: As a young woman and small market trader who struggles to make ends meet selling from a tabletop in her local market. She represents the millions of economically disadvantaged youths in informal trade who need access to markets, financial inclusion, and digital tools to improve their livelihood. To benefit from the digitalization happening around her, Aisha needs training to effectively and safely use digital tools, and she needs digital products and services tailored to her realities as a young woman small trader, so that she can move from the periphery to the center of the digital economy. Social techpreneurs or “Chebet”: A recent university graduate or young social digital entrepreneur who develops inclusive digital solutions responsive to Aisha’s realities. She embodies the entrepreneurial spirit of university educated youth eager to leverage digital innovation for social impact but needs support to succeed. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she has limited financial, technical, and business support to pursue social entrepreneurship. Chebet’s success is directly connected to Aisha because her enterprise is intended, first and foremost, to develop inclusive digital solutions tailored to the needs and realities of small traders such as Aisha. Unemployed disadvantaged youth or “Nala”: Nala is a young person from a low-income household who faces difficulty accessing meaningful employment and seeks ICT training to improve her work prospects. She represents the youth seeking to acquire digital skills to improve their employability and access opportunities in the growing digital economy. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she is from a low-income community and not able to find a job easily. With access to relevant training, certification and employment pathways, she could find better work as tech worker or even upskill her current tech skills to obtain industry-related certification and employment pathways in the emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data science and coding etc. 1.2.3 SAMA Programme Interventions Intervention 1: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation: This intervention focuses on supporting young social techpreneurs like Chebet pursue entrepreneurship to develop homegrown digital solutions that respond to the market barriers experienced by small traders like Aisha to stay in business and thrive in digital markets. Chebet groups will receive relevant digital, tech and entrepreneurship skilling and training. The Programme will support 200 young social techpreneurs to pursue entrepreneurship and develop approximately 80 digital solutions that enable small traders to remain in business, access markets and participate more effectively in the digital economy. This will be carried out in Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Ghana. Intervention 2 – Skilling Young Talents for employability and future of work. This intervention focuses on developing the digital skills of 48,000 young people in Benin and Zambia to prepare them for the future of work either as digital entrepreneurs or tech talent. It comprises two distinct skilling pathways: foundational digital-literacy, financial-literacy and entrepreneurship training for 30,000 small traders like Aisha delivered in-person. While advanced digital skills modules such as cybersecurity, AI, Cloud, data science etc) will be delivered in a hybrid format to 18,000 disadvantaged young people like Nala. Intervention 3 – Strengthening institutions and policy This intervention focuses on enabling policy and regulatory environment to drive inclusive digital transformation across Africa in which the digital innovation and skills interventions can translate into improved economic participation and work opportunities, particularly for young women small traders like Aisha. This intervention works with governments, regulators, and regional bodies to strengthen institutional capacity, develop inclusive policies and regulations, address barriers within digital markets, and advance policy harmonization and interoperability. Consultancy Purpose and Objectives 2.1 Purpose of this Assignment Digital markets, including mobile money, digital payments, e-commerce, social commerce, logistics platforms and other technology-enabled services—can enable informal micro and small traders to reach wider markets, improve transaction efficiency, strengthen customer relationships and increase the resilience and growth of their enterprises. However, participation in and sustained use of these services remain uneven, particularly among economically disadvantaged young women operating within informal and small-scale trade. Young women small traders like Aisha face interconnected barriers that drive them to the margins of digital economy. These may include limited access to affordable digital devices and connectivity, low digital and financial literacy, inadequate access to finance, limited trust in digital platforms, exposure to fraud and online harm, unsuitable platform design, logistics constraints, restrictive social norms, care responsibilities and limited access to appropriate learning and business-support services. These barriers affect not only whether traders adopt digital tools, but also whether they can use them safely, productively, and consistently to improve their livelihoods. Under Intervention 1: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation, SAMA’s implementing partner, GrowthAfrica Foundation, will support 200 young social techpreneurs like Chebet through ideation, incubation and acceleration to develop approximately 80 homegrown digital solutions that respond to the market barriers experienced by informal micro and small traders like Aisha. Without robust evidence on the small traders’ lived experiences, existing behaviours, unmet needs and market conditions, there is a risk that innovation activities may be based on assumptions or produce solutions that are not sufficiently relevant, accessible, affordable or responsive to the target users’ realities. SAMA therefore requires country-specific evidence on how informal micro and small traders currently participate in digital markets; the products and services they use, attempt to use or abandon; the barriers affecting adoption and sustained use; and the market opportunities that inclusive digital solutions could address. The findings will be translated into prioritised challenge areas, problem statements, design criteria, personas and user journeys for use by GrowthAfrica and the Chebet cohorts during ideation, hackathons, incubation and acceleration. Under Intervention 2: Skilling Young Talents for Employability and the Future of Work, SAMA seeks to strengthen the digital, financial and entrepreneurial capabilities required by young people to participate in the digital economy. For this assignment, the Digital Skills Gap Assessment shall examine foundational competencies for Aisha-aligned small traders and advanced digital skills and employment-readiness needs for Nala-aligned disadvantaged youth. For Nala, it shall also assess realistic pathways from training into work, particularly in Benin and Zambia. The assessment is required to establish the digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies currently possessed by different seller segments; identify the skills gaps that constrain digital-market participation; assess the relevance, accessibility and quality of existing skilling provision; and recommend appropriate competency levels, learning pathways, curriculum priorities, delivery modalities, partnerships and inclusion and safeguarding measures. The findings will directly inform the design and contextualisation of seller-focused skilling interventions implemented by NetOne Foundation in Zambia and Pigier Foundation in Benin. For Nala-aligned youth, the findings will also inform how the advanced digital-skills training offered by NetOne Foundation and Pigier Foundation can connect to verified job opportunities and appropriate employer or placement partners. The two evidence needs are closely interconnected. Digital solutions may fail to achieve adoption where traders lack the necessary skills, confidence, devices, trust, or ongoing support. Similarly, digital-skilling interventions may have limited effect where available products, platforms and services are unaffordable, inaccessible, unsafe, or poorly adapted to traders’ realities. Assessing these dimensions through one coordinated consultancy will enable SAMA to develop a coherent evidence base connecting trader needs, digital-market barriers, solution-development opportunities and digital-skilling priorities. Because the evidence needs of Interventions 1 and 2 are closely connected, this assignment will be implemented as a one multi-country consultancy comprising of two distinct, but interrelated components delivered under a single contract: Component 1: Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis among small traders Component 2: Digital Skills Gap Assessment of small traders Both components shall use common definitions and a shared analytical framework to allow comparison across countries and between the two interventions. In addition to generating evidence for programme design, the assignment shall establish baseline reference values for SAMA indicators and outcome domains that can be validly measured through the Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis and the Digital Skills Gap Assessment. These will include digital-market participation and adoption, digital readiness, digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies, access and inclusion barriers, and other relevant pre-intervention conditions. The findings will inform refinement of the SAMA MEL framework and subsequent participant-level baseline measurement. The strategic value of this assignment is to create a common evidence base linking market barriers, user needs, digital-solution opportunities and skills requirements, so that Interventions 1 and 2 reinforce each other rather than operate as separate workstreams. 2.2. Objectives of the assignment The overall objective is to generate a comprehensive, actionable and comparable evidence across the six SAMA countries, on digital-market adoption, barriers, unmet needs and opportunities among small traders (like Aisha) and on the digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills required by formal and informal sellers for effective participation in digital markets; and to translate the findings into design-ready inputs for inclusive digital solutions, competency-based skilling interventions and establish relevant baseline reference values to strengthen the SAMA programme MEL framework; and identify viable post-training employment pathways for Nala-aligned youth, including the skills, credentials and support needed to access them. 2.2.1 Specific Objective The specific objectives of the assignment are to: Map the current state of digital market adoption among informal micro and small traders in each SAMA country, including the digital platforms, products and services currently used, attempted or abandoned. Identify, segment and prioritize barriers, unmet needs and market opportunities affecting micro and small traders’ adoption and sustained use of digital markets, including structural, financial, social, technical, gender-related, accessibility, safety, policy and regulatory barriers factors, and assess the relevance and suitability of existing digital solutions. Translate the digital-market findings into design-ready inputs for inclusive innovation, including validated thematic challenge areas, sector-by-theme matrices, prioritized problem statements, design considerations, personas and user journeys to inform Intervention 1’s hackathon tracks, challenge briefs and incubation support for “Chebet” cohorts. Assess the foundational digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies of Aisha-aligned small traders, and the advanced digital-skills and employment-readiness needs of Nala-aligned disadvantaged youth, taking into account differences across countries and beneficiary segments (disaggregated by sex, age, disability status, displacement status, seller type and location.) Assess the existing digital-skilling ecosystem for both pathways, including training providers, curricula, certification options, employer demand and partnership opportunities, and identify gaps and overlaps affecting learner progression. Develop a practical competency framework prioritized and country-contextualized recommendations translating the identified gaps into competency levels, learning pathways, priority training modules, delivery modalities, targeting, sequencing, partnerships, inclusion measures and monitoring indicators. Identify and assess viable post-training job pathways for Nala-aligned youth in Benin and Zambia, informed by employer and industry demand, entry-level roles, hiring requirements, recruitment channels, work quality and the barriers facing young women and other underserved youth; recommend practical links between SAMA training, certification and access to work. Establish baseline reference values for relevant SAMA indicators and outcome domains measurable through the two assessments, with appropriate definitions and disaggregation, and provide recommendations for their integration into the SAMA MEL Framework. Scope of the Assignment The assignment shall be implemented as one coordinated, multi-country consultancy comprising two distinct but interrelated components. Component 1: Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis among small traders Component 2: Digital Skills Gap Assessment of small traders Both components shall cover Benin, Zambia, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda; and shall generate country-specific findings, cross-country comparisons and consolidated recommendations. In addition to the diagnostic requirements under each Component, the consultant shall establish baseline reference values for relevant SAMA indicators and outcome domains that can be validly measured through the two assessments. Baseline measures shall be embedded within the respective Work Packages rather than undertaken as a separate study. Indicators requiring longitudinal tracking of actual SAMA participants or supported enterprises shall be baselined separately at enrolment, prior to substantive programme support. The consultant shall support this process by developing or refining the relevant participant and enterprise intake tools as part of the MEL alignment component. The assessment shall also generate relevant baseline reference values on digital-market participation, adoption, inclusion and related enterprise-market conditions that support SAMA’s impact pathway and MEL framework. title: Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Consultancy Services to Assess and Address the Policy, Regulatory and Interoperability Barriers That Prevent Young People From Participating in Digital Markets
raw_text: TERMS OF REFERENCE Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Consultancy Services to Assess and Address the Policy, Regulatory and Interoperability Barriers that Prevent Young People from Participating in Digital Markets (KYC, Digital e-Services, Interoperability and Data Exchange across Six African CountriesUnder the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme) Client Smart Africa Secretariat 10th Floor, Career Centre Building KG 541 ST, Kigali, Rwanda, P.O. Box: 4913 Tel: +250 788 300 581/+250788822155 Email: tenderenquiries@smartafrica.org | www.smartafrica.org Source of Funds Mastercard Foundation Programme Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Countries Covered Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia Country of Contract Rwanda RFP No. 158/S.A/RFP/10/2026 Release Date 08/10/2026 Closing Date 09/11/2026 at 17:00 Kigali time (CAT / UTC+2) Enquiries Enquiries: tenderenquiries@smartafrica.org |Submissions: procurement@smartafrica.org 1. About Smart Africa The Smart Africa Alliance is a bold and innovative commitment from African Heads of State and Government to accelerate sustainable socio-economic development on the continent, with the vision of transforming Africa into a Single Digital Market by 2030. Established through its Manifesto, a collaborative effort among African nations, the African Union, the Economic Commission for Africa, the African Development Bank, the World Bank, the International Telecommunication Union, the private sector, and academic and research institutions, the Alliance was endorsed by African leaders in 2014 and has since garnered the support of 42 African countries representing over one billion people. The Smart Africa Secretariat, headquartered in Kigali, Rwanda, coordinates continental programmes that support digital market integration, policy harmonization, institutional strengthening, and innovation-ecosystem development across Member States, placing information and communications technologies at the core of national and continental socio-economic development. More information: https://smartafrica.org 2. The Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme Smart Africa Alliance curated the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA), an initiative that brings in nexus between digital innovation – entrepreneurship, digital skills and knowledge, and strengthening policy and regulatory environment for digitization of markets while impacting youth with a particular focus on young women. SAMA Programme is a four-year, multi-country initiative supported by the Mastercard Foundation, running from 2026 through 2029. The Program aims to unlock dignified and fulfilling work opportunities for 35,584 young people, with a target of 70% young women, 5% persons with disabilities, and 5% refugees/internally displaced persons, by improving access to digital markets for economically disadvantaged youth, particularly young women small traders. The Programme is implemented across six countries: Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia. The program responds to systemic challenges in Africa’s informal economy, where approximately 90% of workers are informal and youth, who make up 75% of the population, face interlinked barriers such as limited digital connectivity, financial exclusion, inadequate market access, and digital skills gaps. SAMA builds on Smart Africa’s existing digital initiatives such as SANIA, SADA, SATA, SWG etc and aligns with the organisation’s vision for Africa’s Single Digital Market by 2030 as well as the African Union’s vision, ensuring that program efforts complement broader continental strategies for inclusive digital transformation. 2.1 SAMA Strategic Pillars SAMA is built around three interconnected strategic pillars to drive inclusive growth: a) Entrepreneurship and digital innovation, b) Youth Digital Skills, and c) Institutional Capacity Building. In practice, this translates to: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation bysupporting youth-led tech solutions that reduce market barriers for informal traders. Youth Digital Skills Development byproviding digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills training to young persons, especially young women, to improve their employability and enterprise growth. Strengthening Institutions and Policy by workingwith governments and regional bodies to harmonize policies, improve regulatory environments, and build institutional capacity for a unified digital market. 2.2 SAMA Target Personas The Programme’s human-centred design is built around and targets three distinct groups of young persons in Africa: Small market trader or “Aisha”: Asa young woman and small market trader who struggles to make ends meet selling from a tabletop in her local market. She represents the millions of economically disadvantaged youths in informal trade who need access to markets, financial inclusion, and digital tools to improve their livelihood. To benefit from the digitalization happening around her, Aisha needs training to effectively and safely use digital tools, and she needs digital products and services tailored to her realities as a young woman small trader, so that she can move from the periphery to the center of the digital economy. Social techpreneurs or “Chebet”: A recent university graduate or young social digital entrepreneur who develops inclusive digital solutions responsive to Aisha’s realities. She embodies the entrepreneurial spirit of university educated youth eager to leverage digital innovation for social impact but needs support to succeed. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she has limited financial, technical, and business support to pursue social entrepreneurship. Chebet’s success is directly connected to Aisha because her enterprise is intended, first and foremost, to develop inclusive digital solutions tailored to the needs and realities of small traders such as Aisha. Unemployed disadvantaged youth or “Nala”: Nala is a young person from a low-income household who faces difficulty accessing meaningful employment and seeks ICT training to improve her work prospects. She represents the youth seeking to acquire digital skills to improve their employability and access opportunities in the growing digital economy. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she is from a low-income community and not able to find a job easily. With access to relevant training, certification and employment pathways, she could find better work as tech worker or even upskill her current tech skills to obtain industry-related certification and employment pathways in the emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data science and coding etc. 2.3 SAMA Programme Interventions Intervention 1: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation: This intervention focuses on supporting young social techpreneurs like Chebet pursue entrepreneurship to develop homegrown digital solutions that respond to the market barriers experienced by small traders like Aisha to stay in business and thrive in digital markets. Chebet groups will receive relevant digital, tech and entrepreneurship skilling and training. The Programme will support 200 young social techpreneurs to pursue entrepreneurship and develop approximately 80 digital solutions that enable small traders to remain in business, access markets and participate more effectively in the digital economy. This will be carried out in Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Ghana. Intervention 2 – Skilling Young Talents for employability and future of work. This intervention focuses on developing the digital skills of 48,000 young people in Benin and Zambia to prepare them for the future of work either as digital entrepreneurs or tech talent. It comprises two distinct skilling pathways: foundational digital-literacy, financial-literacy and entrepreneurship training for 30,000 small traders like Aisha delivered in-person. While advanced digital skills modules such as cybersecurity, AI, Cloud, data science etc) will be delivered in a hybrid format to 18,000 disadvantaged young people like Nala. Intervention 3 – Strengthening institutions and policy This intervention focuses on enabling policy and regulatory environment to drive inclusive digital transformation across Africa in which the digital innovation and skills interventions can translate into improved economic participation and work opportunities, particularly for young women small traders like Aisha. This intervention works with governments, regulators, and regional bodies to strengthen institutional capacity, develop inclusive policies and regulations, address barriers within digital markets, and advance policy harmonization and interoperability. 3. About this Assignment 3.1 What we are asking for We want to know, country by country, exactly what stops a young entrepreneur, particularly a young woman from entering a digital market, operating in it, and growing beyond her own locality or national border. We then want to know what to change, who has to change it, and in what order. The subject areas are Know Your Customer (KYC), digital e-services, digital interoperability and data exchange. These are the levers, not the purpose. The purpose is market access and dignified work. 3.2 What already exists and must not be repeated Smart Africa has already undertaken relevant work in adjacent areas, notably through the Institutional Support for Digital Payments and E-commerce Policies for Cross-Border Trade (IDECT) Project and other Secretariat initiatives and assessments listed in Annex A. Annex A lists the reference materials the Secretariat will make available to the selected Consultant. These will also be shared through the RFP data room so that bidders can size their proposals accurately. The Consultant shall start from this material and shall not re-diagnose issues already adequately covered by it. Where the Consultant believes existing findings are outdated or incomplete, it shall say so explicitly and justify any re-assessment. 3.3 The principle that governs the whole assignment Every activity and every deliverable under this assignment must be independently justifiable against SAMA's objective of improving access to digital markets and dignified work opportunities for young people, particularly young women. Where the evidence produced is subsequently useful to other Smart Africa initiatives, that is a benefit — not an additional objective of this assignment. Bidders should read this as a practical instruction. Section 6.1 sets out how we expect this link to be made in every chapter of every report. 4. Overall Objective The overall objective of this assignment is to identify and help remove the policy, regulatory, institutional and technical barriers that prevent young people — particularly young women and youth-led enterprises — from accessing, participating in and earning a living from domestic and cross-border digital markets in the six SAMA countries. The assignment shall assess the current policy, regulatory, institutional and technical landscape for KYC, digital e-services, digital interoperability and data exchange across the six SAMA countries, and translate the findings into harmonized policy guidelines, recommended technical specifications, practical implementation guidance and toolkits, targeted capacity-building interventions, and country-specific action plans with clearly identified institutions responsible for taking agreed actions forward. The assignment shall also generate the policy, regulatory, institutional and ecosystem starting values required for the SAMA Integrated Baseline. These baseline results will provide the pre-intervention reference point for measuring subsequent changes under Intervention 3 and for reporting relevant SAMA and Mastercard Foundation ecosystem and institutional-strengthening indicators. 5. Specific Objectives The Consultant shall: Assess the policy, legal, regulatory, institutional, governance, technical and operational environment for KYC, digital e-services, interoperability and data exchange in each of the six countries, and score each country against the common maturity framework set out in Annex B. Identify the specific barriers that prevent young women and men entrepreneurs from accessing trusted digital services and participating in domestic and cross-border digital markets, and quantify or characterise who is affected and how. Assess the capacity and readiness of policymakers and implementing institutions to deliver and sustain the reforms identified. Develop evidence-based policy harmonization guidelines for KYC, digital e-services, and interoperability and data exchange. Develop recommended technical specifications and implementation guidelines that countries can adopt voluntarily. Develop practical government implementation toolkits that translate the guidelines into concrete policy, regulatory and institutional steps. Develop capacity-building and knowledge-transfer packages addressing the capacity gaps identified. Determine where controlled regulatory experimentation is justified by the diagnosis, and design sandbox frameworks only for those areas. Support adoption: facilitate national validation and dissemination, inter-country peer learning, and the agreement of prioritized country action plans with the institutions expected to lead them. Establish and document baseline values for Intervention 3 using a common six-country assessment framework, including clear definitions, scoring criteria, evidence sources, limitations and country disaggregation, and provide the resulting dataset and indicator documentation to the SAMA MEAL team. 6. Scope of the Assignment The assignment is organized into three Work Packages. Section 6.1 sets out methodology requirements that apply to all three and that bidders must address in their technical proposals. Bidders are encouraged to complement these requirements with innovative, agile and context-responsive approaches that enhance delivery and impact. 6.1 How the work must be done 6.1.1 Follow the market journey Rather than assessing the four technical domains in isolation or applying a single market journey to all beneficiaries, the Consultant shall assess barriers through differentiated pathways reflecting the SAMA beneficiary groups relevant to this assignment. Pathway 1 – Informal and small-scale traders (Aisha): establish/prove identity → meet KYC requirements → register/formalise the business → access a financial account → receive digital payments → access relevant government e-services → access digital marketplaces → reach customers domestically and across borders. Pathway 2 – Youth-led digital enterprises and innovators (Chebet): establish/register the enterprise → meet KYC and regulatory requirements → access digital identity, payments, government e-services, APIs and relevant data → develop and test a digital solution → obtain required regulatory approvals → integrate/interoperate with relevant public and private systems → scale the solution domestically → expand across borders. The Consultant shall assess where policy, regulatory, institutional and technical barriers interrupt each relevant pathway, who is affected, with particular attention to young women, and what reforms are required to enable progression. The pathways shall be refined during inception based on the confirmed SAMA persona-to-country mapping and country context, while maintaining sufficient consistency to support comparison across the six countries. 6.1.2 Report every gap in the same structure Every thematic chapter of every country report shall present its findings in this chain: Gap → practical barrier → who is affected (with attention to young women and youth-led enterprises) → economic or market consequence → recommended action → responsible institution 6.1.3 Keep technical depth proportionate Technical analysis shall be limited to the level of detail needed to explain barriers to digital market access and identify practical actions. Unnecessary technical detail that does not contribute to these outcomes should be avoided. 6.1.4 Use one comparable scoring framework across all six countries The Consultant shall score each country against the 0–4 maturity scale in Annex B. Each score shall carry three things: the score, the verifiable evidence supporting it, and the implication for young women and youth-led enterprises. The Consultant shall specifically coordinate with the SAMA MEAL team during inception to agree the Intervention 3 indicators, definitions, assessment rubric, evidence standards and data-transfer format. This assignment will generate the specialised policy and institutional baseline evidence; the consultant will consolidate it with the wider programme baseline. The coordination arrangement shall avoid duplicate interviews, workshops and data requests while preserving a clear audit trail of source evidence. 6.1.5 Deliver the countries in two waves The six countries shall be assessed in two waves. The first wave shall be used to test the methodology, assessment tools and maturity framework across a range of country contexts. Lessons from the first wave may be used to make limited adjustments before applying the methodology to the second wave. Any adjustment shall be applied consistently across all six countries to preserve comparability. The first wave should include countries representing different levels of digital-market and institutional maturity. 6.1.6 Coordinate with the parallel SAMA consultancy A parallel SAMA assignment (Digital Market Gap Analysis / Digital Skills Gap Assessment) covers the same six countries. Coordination is not optional and shall be operational, not declaratory. The Inception Report shall include a single consolidated six-country stakeholder engagement plan agreed with the parallel consultancy, covering: a single stakeholder mapping per country; a common government entry point; harmonized questionnaires where the same institution type is being asked similar questions; coordinated mission dates with other SAMA activities. the differentiated beneficiary market-pathway framework, including confirmed persona-to-country mapping Coordinate this assignment with other ongoing SAMA consultancies and country-level activities to avoid duplication and stakeholder fatigue. Engagements shall be coordinated so that separate Smart Africa teams do not approach the same senior government official independently within the same quarter. 6.2 Work Package 1 — KYC and Digital e-Services The Consultant shall establish what it currently takes for a young person or a youth-led enterprise to be identified, verified, registered and served digitally in each country, and where that process breaks down. 6.2.1 Desk review Review national policies, laws, regulations, strategies, standards and institutional frameworks covering digital identity, KYC/e-KYC, customer due diligence, risk-based and proportionate KYC, applicable AML/CFT requirements for digital onboarding, electronic identification, electronic transactions, digital signatures and trust services, consumer protection, data protection and privacy, cybersecurity, digital government services, digital financial services and cross-border digital trade. The assessment shall focus on how these requirements operate in practice and whether their application creates disproportionate barriers for young entrepreneurs, informal traders, MSMEs and start-ups. 6.2.2 Institutional mapping Identify the roles, mandates and coordination mechanisms of the institutions that control each step of the journey: ministries responsible for ICT and the digital economy, financial regulators and central banks, data protection authorities, digital identity authorities, telecommunications regulators, business registration authorities, private-sector associations, innovation hubs, financial service providers and development partners. 6.2.3 Barriers facing young people and young women Assess the barriers experienced by young women entrepreneurs, young men entrepreneurs, MSMEs and start-ups in: e-KYC and identity verification; business registration; customer onboarding; access to financial services; digital payments; access to digital public services; and digital trust. Establish which barriers fall disproportionately on young women, and why. 6.2.4 Country engagement Conduct in-country consultations and a national workshop in each of the six countries covering existing KYC frameworks, digital onboarding practice, availability and coverage of digital identity systems, authentication mechanisms, trust services, maturity of digital public services, cross-border recognition of digital identities, and the implementation problems institutions are actually facing. Assess the practical accessibility and usability of priority government e-services relevant to market participation, including business registration and licensing, tax registration, identity-related services and other relevant services. The assessment shall consider eligibility requirements, authentication, digital completion of transactions, payment integration, interoperability with identity and other government systems, accessibility to young women and underserved groups, and whether users must revert to manual or in-person processes. 6.2.5 Data protection: look beyond the law on paper Recording whether a data protection law exists is not sufficient. For each country, assess: the legal framework; whether a data protection authority has been established; its operational capacity; published regulations and guidance; authorisation or notification processes where applicable; supervisory and enforcement practice; and the mechanisms available for data sharing and cross-border transfers. What matters is whether the regulatory environment functions, not whether the statute exists. 6.2.6 Gap analysis Identify legal, regulatory, institutional, governance, technical and operational gaps, reported in the structure required by section 6.1.2. 6.3 Work Package 2 — Interoperability and Data Exchange The Consultant shall assess how well systems and institutions in each country connect to one another and to systems in other countries, and what this means for a young enterprise trying to operate across services, platforms and borders. 6.3.1 Review existing frameworks Review national interoperability frameworks, digital public infrastructure, enterprise architecture, API frameworks, data-sharing policies, cross-border data exchange arrangements, technical standards, digital identity interoperability, payment interoperability and government interoperability initiatives. 6.3.2 Assess the interoperability ecosystem Evaluate governance arrangements, institutional coordination, adoption of technical standards, API maturity, data-exchange mechanisms, use of open standards, cross-border readiness and infrastructure readiness. The assessment shall examine data governance arrangements, including data ownership/stewardship, access rights, consent where applicable, data-sharing agreements, accountability, security and cross-border data-sharing arrangements. Particular attention shall be given to practical access by start-ups and youth-led digital enterprises to government and other relevant APIs, registries, data and DPI. The Consultant shall assess not only whether access is legally or technically permitted, but also the practical conditions of access, including eligibility, onboarding procedures, documentation, authentication, technical integration requirements, costs/fees, testing or sandbox environments, service-level arrangements and other barriers affecting start-ups. 6.3.3 Assess institutional capacity Assess institutional capacity, technical competencies, existing skills, skills gaps, training needs and readiness to operate and sustain interoperable systems. 6.3.4 Consultations Consult government institutions, regulators, private sector, regional organizations, development partners and innovation ecosystem actors. 6.3.5 Gap analysis Identify policy, regulatory, institutional, governance, technical and skills gaps, reported in the structure required by section 6.1.2, and score each country against Annex B. 6.4 Work Package 3 — Harmonization, Implementation Support and Adoption 6.4.1 Policy harmonization guidelines Develop regional policy harmonization guidelines covering KYC, digital identity, digital e-services, digital trust services, interoperability, data exchange and cross-border digital transactions. The guidelines shall set out guiding principles, policy recommendations, institutional responsibilities, governance models, regional alignment and implementation priorities. 6.4.2 Recommended Technical Specifications and Implementation Guidelines The consultant shall develop recommended technical specifications and implementation guidelines for interoperability and data exchange. These outputs are intended to provide practical guidance to participating countries and institutions and shall not create binding technical or regulatory obligations. 6.4.3 Government implementation toolkits Develop practical implementation guides, model operating procedures, implementation checklists, institutional maturity assessment tools, governance templates and monitoring indicators. 6.4.4 Capacity-building packages Prepare training curricula, facilitator guides, participant manuals, presentation materials, case studies, practical exercises and knowledge products, based on the capacity gaps actually identified in WP1 and WP2. 6.4.5 Regulatory experimentation The Consultant shall first identify the national and regional regulatory and policy areas where controlled experimentation would allow youth-led enterprises and innovators to test solutions to the barriers identified. This assessment is a deliverable in its own, and it may conclude that a national or regional sandbox is or is not the right instrument in a given country or context. Where the diagnosis justifies a regulatory sandbox, the Consultant shall develop a Sandbox Framework and Implementation Plan covering governance, eligibility criteria, onboarding and testing procedures, the innovation lifecycle, monitoring and evaluation, safeguards, exit arrangements, priority use cases, and the institutional, technical, human and indicative budgetary requirements for implementation. For each sandbox recommended for implementation, the Consultant shall also prepare draft Technical Terms of Reference (ToRs) for the subsequent recruitment of the sandbox developer/implementer. The ToRs shall define the proposed scope, functional and technical requirements, implementation approach, required expertise, deliverables, indicative implementation schedule and acceptance requirements. This assignment does not include the procurement, recruitment or technical implementation of the sandbox. These activities will be undertaken separately by Smart Africa and/or the relevant host institution following approval of the proposed sandbox framework and ToRs. 6.4.6 Validation, country ownership and dissemination The Consultant shall support the Secretariat to: conduct technical validation of the guidelines, specifications and toolkits with participating countries and stakeholders; give each country the evidence behind its preliminary maturity assessment and a documented opportunity to submit factual corrections and additional evidence before finalization. Country comments shall be recorded. And incorporated for the final technically validations; present the harmonization guidelines to the SAMA Programme Steering Committee for programme-level technical validation; prepare the technical materials the Secretariat needs to pursue endorsement through the applicable Smart Africa governance processes; organize six (6) national dissemination and adoption workshops; facilitate two (2) inter-country peer-learning workshops and online workshops when needed. Each national workshop must end with something concrete. The Consultant shall facilitate and document a prioritised country action plan that identifies the agreed reform actions, the institution(s) that participating country stakeholders confirm are expected to lead follow-up on each action, supporting institutions, indicative sequencing and immediate next steps. Note: The firm should be able to conduct their work in both French and English where needed. The client will not be responsible of hiring for interpretation services in any case 6.5 Baseline Measurement The baseline component shall be embedded across Work Packages and shall measure conditions that exist before SAMA-supported policy harmonisation, capacity building, adoption support or sandbox implementation begins. Implementation outputs that have not yet commenced, including SAMA-developed frameworks, policymakers trained through SAMA and SAMA-supported regulatory sandboxes, shall be recorded as zero rather than treated as contextual baseline measures. The Consultant shall establish the following baseline domains: Policy enabling environment for trusted and inclusive digital markets; KYC and digital-identity policy, regulatory and operational readiness; Digital e-services and electronic trust-services maturity; Digital interoperability and data-exchange maturity, including cross-border readiness; Institutional mandates, coordination, governance, reform ownership and implementation capacity; Policymaker knowledge, competencies, skills gaps and training needs; Regulatory-sandbox readiness, including legal authority, governance, testing, monitoring, safeguards and exit arrangements; and Extent to which the enabling environment addresses barriers experienced by young women entrepreneurs, persons with disabilities and displaced youth. During inception, the Consultant shall propose a standardised indicator reference and maturity-assessment framework for approval by Smart Africa. For every baseline measure, the framework shall specify the definition, unit or rating approach, calculation or scoring method, evidence required, source institution, frequency, responsible party, assumptions, limitations and intended disaggregation. Country results shall be comparable while retaining sufficient narrative explanation of national context. The Consultant shall submit a clean machine-readable baseline dataset, country scorecards, an indicator dictionary, scoring guidance, a source and evidence register, stakeholder mapping, interview and workshop records, and a concise methodological note. All calculations and ratings shall be reproducible from the submitted evidence and shall comply with the assignment's quality assurance and data-protection requirements. The Consultant shall ensure that the maturity assessment is repeatable and maintainable by Smart Africa beyond the assignment. This shall include documented indicators, scoring criteria, evidence requirements and assessor-calibration procedures, alignment with the relevant SAMA Results Framework indicators, and handover of the final assessment tools, editable datasets/templates and update guidance to Smart Africa. 7. Consultant opinion alone is not evidence; the implication — what this score means in practice for young people and young women trying to participate in a digital market.
